bibl.title: Crosslinguistic Corpus Studies in Linguistic Typology

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Corpus-based studies have become increasingly common in linguistic typology over recent years, amounting to the emergence of a new field that we call corpus-based typology.

span.label: corpus-based typology
span.quote: The core idea of corpus-based typology is to take languages as populations of utterances and to systematically investigate text production across languages in this sense.

span.label: review
span.quote: In this article we describe some of the key insights that systematic investigations of language usage—as undertaken in corpus linguistics—contribute to our understanding of diverse and universal aspects of the near 7,000 human languages in the world.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Conventionalised orders minimise total dependency length, and because a dependent tree then sits closer to the higher head it hangs from, harmonic (cross-domain aligned) word order falls out as a by-product.
span.quote: The general conclusion is that DLM as observable in corpora provides an overall explanation for harmonic word order correlations observed in GBT, because head dependency trees occur overall closer to the higher-level heads of which they are dependents.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Keeping a head adjacent to the head of its dependent lets the hearer recognise higher-order constituency sooner, which is why languages converge on harmonic orders.
span.quote: propose that head adjacency as sketched above is preferable for language processing because it allows a recipient to recognize the constituency of higher-order phrases more immediately

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Nouns anchor referring expressions and so open a wider set of lexical and referential choices, making them harder to plan, which shows up as slower speech and pausing just before them.
span.quote: They explain this finding in terms of greater planning difficulties associated with nouns, which serve as the core of referring expressions and whose production thus entails a larger range of lexical and referential choices (Arnold 2008) than is common with verbs.

span.label: The authors' own exploratory comparison of noun-phrase lengths in Universal Dependencies versus Multi-CAST is presented as preliminary.
span.quote: Although more detailed investigations are required, these initial observations suggest that spoken texts fail to exhibit the prerequisite for DLM effects, namely phrases/local dependency trees of sufficient length.

span.label: Corpus representativeness is identified as the field's most pressing unsolved problem.
span.quote: The most pressing issue in CBT is the representativeness of corpora usable for crosslinguistic research.

span.label: Spoken and especially interactional language use is badly under-represented in available corpora.
span.quote: Not only is there a blatant shortage of spoken-language data from a larger range of languages, but there is even less interactional language use (i.e., conversations) represented in any currently available corpora in CBT.

span.label: The review names its field's outstanding problem as the corpora themselves: they are not yet crosslinguistically representative, and spoken or signed texts are what is missing.
span.quote: We also consider remaining challenges for corpus-based typology, in particular the development of crosslinguistically more representative corpora that include spoken (or signed) texts

span.label: The texts that would be comparable are frequently not obtainable, and copyright is named as one of the reasons, so what can be compared is set by access rather than by the research question.
span.quote: However, these kinds of texts are rarely published in the form of organized web-accessible corpora and in many cases are not openly accessible at all

span.label: language - AS A POPULATION OF UTTERANCE TOKENS: the corpus-based conception, in which an individual corpus is a SAMPLE of that population rather than the language itself
span.quote: CBT conceives of languages as populations of utterance tokens and their component parts rather than as monolithic entities shared by all members of a speech community. Individual language corpora are thus samples of utterance populations, each associated with different linguistic conventions.

span.label: language - AS A MONOLITHIC ENTITY shared by all members of a speech community: the conception the corpus-based view is explicitly defined against
span.quote: rather than as monolithic entities shared by all members of a speech community.

span.label: word order - a CATEGORICAL property in some languages and a probabilistic one in most: Tamil at 0% and Arabic at 100% VO, while most languages show variability with a preference
span.quote: First, some languages have absolutely fixed word order rules and these are reflected as categorical distributions, with Tamil, for instance, showing 0% and Arabic 100% VO orders. Although most languages show some variability in VO order, most of these also show a clear preference for one order or the other.

span.label: builds-on → Haig et al. (2011)
span.quote: We term the joint advances of corpus-based studies in linguistic typology corpus-based typology (CBT) (Haig et al. 2011) and contrast it with grammar-based typology (GBT).3

span.label: contradicts → Du Bois (1987) discourse ergativity
span.quote: Investigating a larger range of spoken-language original text corpora from Multi-CAST, Haig & Schnell (2016) and Schnell et al. (2021) do not find support for discourse ergativity

span.label: corpus-based typology —contrasted-with→ grammar-based typology
span.quote: In comparing languages, CBT focuses on variation within languages and seeks to determine (conditioned) structural probabilities, which are then compared across languages. This is in contrast to GBT

span.label: regression
span.quote: The dashed line is a linear regression fit to the data; with an intercept of β0 = 24.77 and a regression coefficient of β1 = 0.84, it is nearly parallel to the central solid line.

span.label: mean
span.quote: The mean individual language corpus size is 131,574 word tokens (SD = 287,554), indicating massive variability in corpus sizes

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: with approximately 36% of NPs [standard deviation (SD) = 15%] being l ≥ 4 dependencies in length in the former and only approximately 12% (SD = 9%) in the latter

span.label: Corpus-based typology largely reproduces the classifications of grammar-based typology, but adds finer-grained, quantitatively explicit detail and robustness.
span.quote: Thus, CBT findings largely confirm GBT findings but lend more empirical detail and robustness to observations of regularities.

span.label: In the authors' own comparison, long noun phrases are far commoner in the written Universal Dependencies corpora (about 36% of NPs at least four dependencies long) than in the spoken Multi-CAST corpora (about 12%).
span.quote: with approximately 36% of NPs [standard deviation (SD) = 15%] being l ≥ 4 dependencies in length in the former and only approximately 12% (SD = 9%) in the latter

span.label: Because spoken texts contain too few phrases long enough for reordering to matter, dependency length minimisation cannot be what drives word order variation in speech.
span.quote: these initial observations suggest that spoken texts fail to exhibit the prerequisite for DLM effects, namely phrases/local dependency trees of sufficient length

span.label: Across 12 spoken corpora, subjects inside a same-subject reference chain are about 15-20% likelier to be realised as zero than subjects elsewhere, regardless of the language's overall zero rate.
span.quote: chain-medial subjects are approximately 15–20% more likely to be zero than other subjects, irrespective of how common zero subjects are in the language overall

span.label: Nearly every language with a zero-subject rate above 70% has fully grammaticalised, transparent subject agreement, the exceptions being Mandarin and Jinghpaw.
span.quote: For instance, almost all languages with rates of zero subjects above 70% have fully grammaticalized and transparent subject agreement, with the exception of the Sino-Tibetan languages Mandarin and Jinghpaw.

span.label: Du Bois's discourse-ergativity hypothesis is not supported by spoken original-text corpora: intransitive subjects (S), not transitive objects (P), show the lowest rate of new-referent and full-NP expression.
span.quote: Haig & Schnell (2016) and Schnell et al. (2021) do not find support for discourse ergativity: While the disinclination of A toward newness and full NP expression is confirmed, they find S to consistently show a lower rate of newness and full NP expression than P.

span.label: Speakers slow their articulation and pause more often before nouns than before verbs, a tendency found across nine typologically diverse spoken corpora.
span.quote: The authors find that slowdown of speech rate, manifested as slower articulation of a word form and greater likelihood of pausing just prior to its articulation, is significantly more likely to occur before nouns than before verbs.

span.label: Word-order entropy trades off against case marking: the less confusable subject and object are by case, the freer their relative order.
span.quote: Levshina finds a negative correlation between the confusability of subject and object in terms of case marking and the entropy of their relative order.

span.label: The largest annotated multilingual resource is typologically skewed - 24 million tokens across 104 languages, more than half of them Indo-European.
span.quote: The UD corpora (version 2.7; Zeman et al. 2020) achieves an impressive overall corpus size of 24 million word tokens; although it covers 104 languages, over half are Indo-European.

span.label: Spoken-language data are scarce in corpus-based typology and conversational interaction is scarcer still, so representative language use remains out of reach.
span.quote: Not only is there a blatant shortage of spoken-language data from a larger range of languages, but there is even less interactional language use (i.e., conversations) represented in any currently available corpora in CBT.

span.label: corpus-based typology (CBT)
span.quote: We term the joint advances of corpus-based studies in linguistic typology corpus-based typology (CBT) (Haig et al. 2011) and contrast it with grammar-based typology (GBT).

span.label: languages as populations of utterance tokens (the core conception of CBT)
span.term: languages as populations of utterance tokens (the core conception of CBT)
span.quote: CBT conceives of languages as populations of utterance tokens and their component parts rather than as monolithic entities shared by all members of a speech community.

span.label: grammar-based typology (GBT)
span.quote: We term this research tradition grammar-based typology (GBT).

span.label: parallel text corpora
span.quote: Parallel text corpora are translational texts that contain exactly parallel content.

span.label: parallax text corpora
span.quote: Parallax text corpora contain responses to the same (nonlinguistic) stimulus (e.g., pictures or picture books, movies) across language users/languages, which yields texts with essentially stable content.

span.label: original text corpora
span.quote: Original text corpora involve free, nontranslational texts uncontrolled for content that are often produced outside of academic linguistic contexts (cf. Haig et al. 2011).

span.label: dependency length minimization (DLM)
span.quote: DLM is a general principle of efficiency in language use that operates in a way similar to Hawkins’s (2004) early immediate constituency principle, as outlined above.

span.label: discourse ergativity
span.quote: this hypothesis, termed discourse ergativity, was based mainly on a corpus of Pear stories from Sakapultek Maya and taken to explain the emergence of ergative alignment in human language grammars in general

span.label: text modality of the corpus (predominantly written vs. entirely spoken)
span.term: text modality of the corpus (predominantly written vs. entirely spoken)
span.quote: We conclude the discussion of word order typology in CBT with a short exploratory examination of constituent lengths in two multilingual corpora, namely UDs and Multi-CAST (Haig & Schnell 2015; cf. Section 3.1). The former consists predominantly of written texts and the latter entirely of spoken texts.

span.label: noun phrase length
span.quote: Multi-CAST contains subcorpora from 15 languages, for which standardized annotations allow us to determine NP length as the sum of all of its contiguous nominal subconstituents.

span.label: proportion of zero subjects (versus pronouns)
span.quote: Figure 2 renders the proportions of zeros (versus pronouns) within (y-axis) and outside of (x-axis) same-subject chains in 12 language corpora from Multi-CAST.

span.label: 36% ... 12% — share of noun phrases at least four dependencies long in the written UD corpora versus the spoken Multi-CAST corpora
span.quote: with approximately 36% of NPs [standard deviation (SD) = 15%] being l ≥ 4 dependencies in length in the former and only approximately 12% (SD = 9%) in the latter

span.label: 15–20% — extra likelihood that a chain-medial subject is zero rather than a pronoun, compared with subjects outside a same-subject chain
span.quote: chain-medial subjects are approximately 15–20% more likely to be zero than other subjects, irrespective of how common zero subjects are in the language overall

span.label: β1 = 0.84 — regression coefficient of the fit relating zero rates inside versus outside same-subject chains, with intercept 24.77
span.quote: The dashed line is a linear regression fit to the data; with an intercept of β0 = 24.77 and a regression coefficient of β1 = 0.84, it is nearly parallel to the central solid line.

span.label: 1,257 — languages covered by the Parallel Bible Corpus, averaging 10,707 verses per language
span.quote: The former contains translations of the Christian New Testament in 1,257 languages, including some underresearched ones; individual language corpora contain an average of 10,707 verses (SD = 7,727)

span.label: 464 — languages for which a Universal Declaration of Human Rights translation exists, averaging 1,694 words each
span.quote: UDHRs are currently available in 464 languages, but are focused on official and typically standard languages (Cysouw & Wälchli 2007), with an estimated average length of 1,694 words for each translation (SD = 500).

span.label: 24 million — word tokens in Universal Dependencies v2.7, spread over 104 languages of which over half are Indo-European
span.quote: The UD corpora (version 2.7; Zeman et al. 2020) achieves an impressive overall corpus size of 24 million word tokens; although it covers 104 languages, over half are Indo-European.

span.label: 131,574 — mean word-token size of an individual language corpus in Universal Dependencies
span.quote: The mean individual language corpus size is 131,574 word tokens (SD = 287,554), indicating massive variability in corpus sizes

span.label: 143 ... 74 — UD corpora, and languages they come from, used in the authors' own NP-length analysis after excluding 37 with under 1,000 data points
span.quote: We consider 143 UD corpora from 74 languages, excluding 37 that yield less than 1,000 data points.
